summary: A 1977 extension to FTP, called XSEN, that provides for sending a message to a logged-in user, with variants for mailing it normally. It adds new FTP commands with syntax like the existing MAIL command.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally email waits in a mailbox. This extension lets a message pop up right on the screen of someone who is logged in.

questions: send message to logged in user ftp
subtitle: Send a message directly to a user's terminal over FTP, or mail it if they are not logged in

tldr.problem: On some systems, users could send messages directly to someone else's terminal if they were logged in, but this only worked locally. Extending this across the network required new FTP commands.
tldr.mechanism: The XSEN extension adds three new FTP commands with the same syntax as the existing MAIL command: XSEN (send to terminal only), XSEM (send, mail if can't), and XMAS (mail and send). The server returns different reply codes depending on success and whether the message was sent versus mailed.
tldr.outcome: Inter-system message sending became possible on systems with the extension, though implementations on ITS and SAIL were limited to short messages and did not extend to MLFL (mail file) mode.

today: RFC 737 is an Unknown status experimental protocol from October 1977 for FTP message extensions. The commands were implemented on MIT ITS and SAIL systems but did not become part of standard FTP.

sections.title: Remote Terminal Messaging
sections.content:
Several computers in the network—notably SAIL (SU-AI) and ITS systems at MIT—had a local SEND command that could dispatch a message directly to a user's terminal. RFC 737 extends this idea to the network: three new FTP commands allow sending messages between sites.

The commands have the same syntax as the existing MAIL command, making them familiar to implementors already using FTP for mail.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds new commands to FTP so one computer can push a message straight to someone's terminal on another computer.

sections.title: The Three New Commands
sections.content:
XSEN sends a message directly to the recipient's terminal. If the user is not logged in or is refusing messages, the server returns a 453 failure reply.

XSEM (Send, Mail if can't) attempts to send the message to the terminal, but if that fails, it falls back to mailing the message. It returns a 009 notification reply if the send failed but the mail succeeded.

XMAS (Mail And Send) does both: it attempts to send to the terminal and also mails the message, with no special distinction between success modes. The humor in the name was intentional.
sections.plainLanguage: XSEN tries to put it on someone's screen. XSEM tries the screen first, then emails it. XMAS does both. Each has different reply codes to say what happened.

sections.title: Implementation Constraints
sections.content: These commands are designed for short messages only. The RFC notes that neither the ITS nor SAIL implementations provides variants for MLFL (mail file), because the extended messages from MLFL mode are too large for this use case. The design prioritizes simplicity and the interactive, conversational nature of terminal messages over bulk message handling.
sections.plainLanguage: These commands work best for quick notes, not long files. That is why they did not add support for the bigger message mode.

references.text: Postel, J. and Reynolds, J., "File Transfer Protocol", STD 9, RFC 959, October 1985.
